content: Methimazole or propylthiouracil may be administered to inhibit the synthesis of thyroid hormones. This is typically followed, within one to two hours, by the administration of large doses of iodine to inhibit both the synthesis and release of thyroid hormones. Glucocorticoids may also be used to inhibit the peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3). In cases where clinical deterioration persists despite conventional therapy, advanced interventions such as plasmapheresis, charcoal hemoperfusion, or exchange transfusion may be considered. Due to the high protein-binding nature of T4, dialysis is not effective in removing significant amounts of the hormone. The synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones are regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis. Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), secreted by the hypothalamus, stimulates the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). TSH, in turn, acts on the thyroid gland to stimulate the production and release of thyroid hormones, primarily L-thyroxine (T4) and L-triiodothyronine (T3). Circulating levels of T3 and T4 exert a feedback effect on TRH and TSH secretion. Elevated levels of T3 and T4 suppress TRH and TSH secretion, while decreased levels stimulate their release. The physiological actions of thyroid hormones are thought to be mediated primarily through the regulation of DNA transcription and protein synthesis. T3 and T4 enter the cell nucleus and bind to thyroid receptor proteins attached to DNA, activating gene transcription and the synthesis of messenger RNA and cytoplasmic proteins. Thyroid hormones play a critical role in regulating metabolic processes, supporting normal growth and development, and ensuring proper maturation of the central nervous system and bone. Their metabolic effects include increased cellular respiration, thermogenesis, and the metabolism of proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids. The anabolic effects of thyroid hormones are essential for normal growth and development. The majority of the physiological effects of thyroid hormones are attributed to T3, with approximately 80% of T3 being derived from the peripheral conversion of T4. Synthroid (levothyroxine sodium tablets, USP) contains synthetic crystalline L-3,3',5,5'-tetraiodothyronine sodium salt, which is chemically identical to the T4 produced by the human thyroid gland. The structural formula of synthetic T4 is identical to that of endogenous T4. The pharmacokinetics of levothyroxine include absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination. Oral absorption of T4 ranges from 40% to 80%, with the majority being absorbed in the jejunum and upper ileum. Fasting increases T4 absorption, while malabsorption syndromes, certain foods (e.g., soybean infant formula), and dietary fiber decrease its bioavailability. Absorption may also decline with age. Synthroid tablets have a relative bioavailability of approximately 93% compared to oral levothyroxine sodium solution. Thyroid hormones are more than 99% bound to plasma proteins, including thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), thyroxine-binding prealbumin (TBPA), and albumin. TBG and TBPA have a higher affinity for T4, contributing to its higher serum levels, slower metabolic clearance, and longer half-life compared to T3. Only the unbound (free) hormone is metabolically active. Various drugs and physiological conditions can affect the binding of thyroid hormones to serum proteins. Thyroid hormones do not readily cross the placental barrier. The metabolism of T4 occurs primarily through sequential deiodination, with approximately 80% of circulating T3 derived from peripheral T4 by monodeiodination. The liver is the primary site of degradation for both T4 and T3, although deiodination also occurs in the kidneys and other tissues. About 80% of the daily T4 dose is deiodinated to produce equal amounts of T3 and reverse T3 (rT3). Both T3 and rT3 are further deiodinated to diiodothyronine. Thyroid hormones are also metabolized via conjugation with glucuronides and sulfates and excreted into the bile and gut, where they undergo enterohepatic recirculation. Thyroid hormones are primarily eliminated by the kidneys, with a portion of the conjugated hormone excreted unchanged in the feces. Approximately 20% of T4 is eliminated in the stool. Urinary excretion of T4 decreases with age. Animal studies have not been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic, mutagenic, or fertility effects of levothyroxine. Synthetic T4 in Synthroid is identical to the T4 naturally produced by the human thyroid gland. While there have been reports of an association between prolonged thyroid hormone therapy and breast cancer, this has not been confirmed. Patients receiving Synthroid for appropriate clinical indications should be titrated to the lowest effective replacement dose. Synthroid tablets are round, color-coded, scored, and debossed with SYNTHROID on one side and the potency on the other. They should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). The tablets must be protected from light and moisture.
